## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{20}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why can handing a moving robot to a human operator cause the collision the handover was meant to prevent?_

Most deployed robots keep a person in reserve for the situations their learned policies cannot handle, and that reserve is usually treated as the final safeguard. A person, however, needs a large fraction of a second to respond even while watching closely and several seconds after only monitoring, and a machine moving at walking pace covers meters in that time, so a request for help can consume the very clearance the help was meant to protect. Taking over also creates hazards of its own. Two controllers that each believe they hold a joint can command it at once, a controller that believes the other still holds it can leave it unattended, and an abrupt switch between their commands jolts the drivetrain and the load it carries. A takeover that grants unchecked control lets a startled or lagging operator drive the machine into a rack, and a log that does not mark who commanded each instant can neither settle what caused an incident nor keep the machine's own near-failures out of the demonstrations it later learns from. Authority can change hands within a single control cycle, but the momentum already delivered across the causal boundary cannot be recalled, so a takeover must be engineered as a control action with its own deadline, its own limits, and its own record.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Specify operator permissions through capability matrices that bind each authenticated role's operations to physical channels, preemption tiers, and clearance-derived deadlines
- Select a state-dependent local fallback that remains physically feasible while human intervention is pending
- Evaluate the inherited chunk lease and the chosen manual lease against their modes' stopping reserves and available fallback mechanisms
- Calculate the latest fallback time and takeover speed ceilings from human reaction latency and remaining physical stopping clearance
- Design authority handshakes that keep one owner on each actuator output and size fixed-endpoint $C^2$ command blends within each channel's rate limit
- Formulate the four temporal intervals of causal intervention masking to isolate policy drift, enforcer blends, and human stabilization in imitation learning datasets
- Evaluate whether an authority record provides the cryptographic and kinematic evidence needed to reconstruct post-incident fault causality

:::

## Shared Authority {#sec-intervention-shared-authority}

Supervisory intervention is the transfer of the right to propose actions from a learned policy to a person and, later, back again. Nearly every physical AI system in service depends on it. Remote assistants resolve the blocked aisles and ambiguous scenes that warehouse robots and driverless vehicles cannot, safety drivers and pendant operators take over when a policy leaves the conditions it was built for, and the corrections they make become training data for the next policy. Block diagrams draw the supervisor as a single arrow into the plant. A moving machine, however, does not pause while that arrow changes source, so a handover is not an interface event but a control action with a physical deadline, performed by the slowest and least predictable component in the loop.

The chapter's central question is how authority can change hands on a moving machine without spending clearance the machine does not have, without two controllers commanding one actuator, and without losing the evidence of who commanded each instant. The principle that governs Part IV frames the answer (\ref{pri-vol4-evidence-bounds-authority}). A person's authority, like the policy's, is granted on evidence and expires with it, and every command the person issues remains a proposal that the permission path checks before it crosses the causal boundary. The sections that follow take a takeover in the order it unfolds: who may act on which physical channel, how long the machine can afford to wait, how ownership of each channel commits, how the command changes without a jolt, how the operator is authenticated, and how the event is recorded so that it can be reconstructed and learned from.

```{python}
#| label: calc-intervention-shared-authority-scene
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ OPENING SCENE: A TWO-SECOND PAUSE AT AISLE SPEED
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-intervention-shared-authority, first paragraph.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that an out-of-loop pause outruns the rack-end clear distance.
# │ Show:    Aisle speed, design out-of-loop takeover delay, travel, clear distance.
# │ How:     WarehouseAisle scenario fields; the design takeover is the 90th
# │          percentile condition-mean take-over time plus transport
# │          (AISLE.t_takeover_out_of_loop); travel = v * T_takeover.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import meter, second, millisecond
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_velocity, fmt_length, fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class InterventionSharedAuthorityScene:
    """Travel during an out-of-loop takeover pause at the aisle speed."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
    t_pause = AISLE.t_takeover_out_of_loop  # category: derived (sourced p90 take-over time + transport)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    permission_rate = RM.permission_rate  # category: chosen
    tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen (from RM.permission_rate)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    travel = (v * t_pause).to(meter)
    travel_ratio = (travel / d_clear).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(travel.magnitude - 5.8045) < 5e-4, f"travel during the pause: {travel}")
    check(travel > 5 * d_clear, "The pause must carry the machine more than five times the clear distance.")
    check(abs((tick * permission_rate).to("").magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "The permission tick is one period of the permission loop.")
    check(abs(tick.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "Canon: 1 kHz permission loop, 1 ms tick.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    t_pause_str = fmt_latency(t_pause, unit=second, precision=1)
    travel_str = fmt_length(travel, unit=meter, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    chunk_lease_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    permission_rate_str = fmt_frequency(permission_rate, precision=0)
    tick_str = fmt_latency(tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
```

On the warehouse mobile manipulator the constraint is immediate. When a pallet blocks an aisle, the machine needs a remote assistant to take over, yet at its chosen `{python} InterventionSharedAuthorityScene.v_str` aisle speed a `{python} InterventionSharedAuthorityScene.t_pause_str` pause before braking, the sourced out-of-loop takeover time of @sec-intervention-reaction-drift, would carry it `{python} InterventionSharedAuthorityScene.travel_str`, more than five times its `{python} InterventionSharedAuthorityScene.d_clear_str` rack-end clear distance. An operator request reaches a machine that is already moving under an admitted command; it cannot erase momentum or make an actuator respond instantaneously. The arbiter, the permission path's source-selection step, must decide who may propose the next command, and the enforcer, its admission check, must admit or reject it; both run deterministically on the safety microcontroller (MCU). The plant must still have enough clearance to execute the chosen stop. An abrupt setpoint switch requests an instantaneous torque step that the motor drives, gearboxes, and payload must absorb. A delayed switch can exhaust stopping room even when both the learned policy and the human controller are individually well behaved.

The base's momentum and kinetic energy remain on the far side of the causal boundary (@sec-boundary-causal-boundary), and the plant keeps evolving under its last admitted command while the operator reconstructs the scene. That reconstruction is slow for reasons Bainbridge named in her *ironies of automation* [@bainbridge1983ironies]. A designer who automates to remove the operator still leaves the operator the tasks that could not be automated, which are the abnormal ones. An operator who has only monitored has lost the manual skill and the running picture of the plant that a fast takeover needs, so a person who must act quickly acts on minimal information. Automation also relies on that operator to watch for rare failures, a task no person sustains for long. The out-of-the-loop literature has since measured both halves of the argument. Passive monitoring degrades situation awareness[^fn-situation-awareness-levels] and slows decisions after an automation failure [@endsley1995outofloop], and complacency appears whenever other work competes for the monitor's attention [@parasuraman2010complacency]. The machine must therefore preserve its own stopping envelope throughout human re-engagement. Faster communication cannot remove the time needed to recognize a hazard, decide, and move the controls.

[^fn-situation-awareness-levels]: **Situation Awareness Levels**\index{Situation awareness!three levels}: @endsley1995toward set out situation awareness as three levels: perceiving the elements of a scene, comprehending what they mean together, and projecting their state forward. The levels fail separately. A remote assistant can see the pallet without projecting that the base will not stop short of it, which is why a console that reports where the operator is looking cannot shorten the response budget (@sec-intervention-failure-modes).

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The proposal boundary of @sec-boundary-machine-model, and the third law in @sec-boundary-bedrock-laws that it enforces, set the baseline for supervisory preemption.
:::

The state-dependent fallback of @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder governs every stage. A moving base may require powered deceleration followed by brake application at standstill; a loaded arm may require a supported hold. Both depend on the sensing and energy sources qualified for that response. Local damping, torque inhibit, and supply isolation are different actions and cannot be substituted for the selected stop by arranging them in a universal escalation ladder. A trusted protective input invokes its separately validated plant response.

Autonomous and manual proposal rights have separate leases. The autonomous action-chunk lease remains the running machine's lease from @sec-nervous-cadences; the manual session receives a clearance-budgeted manual lease. Rejecting an invalid replacement does not revoke an active command whose own evidence, state, and lease remain valid. Expiry or loss of those premises invokes the applicable local fallback.

The permission path resolves split-brain command contention through a source arbiter and **exclusive actuator-output ownership**. In this chapter's `{python} InterventionSharedAuthorityScene.permission_rate_str` controller, commit revokes the policy's logical proposal token and latches its last approved reference; the enforcer remains the sole actuator writer before, during, and after the transition. Controller Area Network (CAN) bus arbitration can serialize traffic from several senders without establishing which sender has control authority. The hazard is that validly transmitted but conflicting commands reach the same actuator. Qualified output gating and source selection must prevent that conflict. In continuous dynamics, the enforcer executes a bumpless transfer (a command handoff with no step in the actuator reference, @sec-intervention-bumpless-transfer) between the checked endpoints under the channel's command-rate and measured plant limits.

Intervention events also reach the core machine learning lifecycle. A rescued episode logged without its handover instant looks like an expert demonstration of the very near-failure states that made the rescue necessary. @Sec-data-intervention-recovery explains why the learner-visited states before a takeover are worth keeping and why the learner's commands there are not; the learning methods that consume interventions, from DAgger [@ross2011reduction] to its human-gated successors (@sec-intervention-recovery-eligibility), all need to know which controller owned each sample. This requires the chapter's formal deliverable, the **authority record**\index{Authority record} (the twelfth record in the record chain), to preserve the complete evidentiary trace from before the takeover. Its per-tick authority log therefore timestamps every authority transition on the safety microcontroller's clock. The commit instant ends policy ownership; the subsequent enforcer blend and reviewed human recovery remain distinct intervals.

The first design decision fixes which named intervention may reach which physical channel, and how long the machine can wait for it; the handshake, the blend, and the record are all built on that grant.

## Human Authority, Reaction Time, and Clearance {#sec-intervention-human-authority}

An assistant guiding the arm can move the chassis if its credential also permits base-drive commands. A command admitted under that permission performs mechanical work on the plant before software can revoke it. Authority must therefore identify the physical channels a person may affect, rather than grant unrestricted access through a generic operator role.

The remote assistant who clears a blocked aisle and the coworker who takes an item from the gripper act on the same machine, and neither should hold the other's authority. Each grant therefore names an operation together with its timing budget, physical degrees of freedom, and preemption rule. The permission path keeps these grants in an explicit **capability matrix**\index{Capability matrix}, a permissions table mapping individual operations (such as an emergency power cutoff, a velocity trim adjustment, a trajectory path veto, or manual drive of the base and arm) to authenticated roles, reflecting classic taxonomies of human supervisory control[^fn-std-sheridan-supervisory] [@sheridan1992telerobotics] and multi-level automation [@parasuraman2000model]. Each entry in this matrix defines the exact actuator channels the operation governs, the preemption tier it carries over the learned policy, and the maximum propagation latency permitted from physical input to actuator response.

[^fn-std-sheridan-supervisory]: **Supervisory Control Levels**\index{Supervisory Control Levels}: @sheridan1978human formulated a ten-level taxonomy of supervisory control, running from a human who performs the whole task without computer assistance to a computer that decides and acts while ignoring the human. A capability matrix draws such distinctions per operation rather than once for the whole machine.

Sheridan also describes the supervisor's work as five steps in sequence: plan the task off-line, teach the plan to the computer, monitor the automatic action, intervene when it fails or the goal changes, and learn from the episode [@sheridan2021supervisory]. This chapter engineers the fourth step and records the evidence the fifth needs. His taxonomy of levels, by contrast, assigns one level to a whole task. The mobile manipulator needs a level per channel and per instant. During a takeover the arm can sit near the manual end of the scale while the base still runs at the automatic end, and the enforcer holds the automatic end on every channel throughout, because it admits the operator's commands exactly as it admits the policy's. That split is where supervisory control becomes a systems problem. Levels that differ across channels are what a supervisor can lose track of, the mode confusion of @sec-intervention-failure-modes, so every level change must be committed and announced per channel.

Naming the operations separates intervention from **safety enforcement**\index{Safety enforcement}, two mechanisms that system architectures routinely conflate. Enforcement withholds permission from a candidate action proposed by a learned model, modifying, clamping, or projecting the setpoint while leaving the machine under autonomous control. Intervention transfers authority away from the model to an external entity, terminating autonomous operation and giving the supervisor the right to propose, while every command still passes the permission path. An **enforcement filter**\index{Enforcement filter} sits in the fast inner control loop (`{python} InterventionSharedAuthorityScene.permission_rate_str` / $\le$ `{python} InterventionSharedAuthorityScene.tick_str`) to prevent the policy from demanding an over-current maneuver or violating a barrier certificate [@ames2019control] during nominal tracking, respecting the actuator thermal limits established in @sec-body-five-budgets and the kinodynamic feasibility boundaries from @sec-planning-kinodynamic-feasibility. An intervention mechanism strips the policy of its proposal token when an operational boundary is breached or an operator demands control. A system equipped with enforcement but lacking intervention cannot be redirected when human intent changes or external conditions fall outside the policy design envelope, leading to conservative deadlock when barrier constraints collapse the feasible control set. Conversely, a system equipped with intervention but lacking enforcement permits a lagging operator to drive the plant into structural failure during nominal manual operation. @Tbl-14-enforcement-vs-intervention summarizes the architectural boundaries between these two protective mechanisms without changing the selected physical fallback.

| Dimension            | Enforcement filter                                                                                                                                     | Intervention state machine                                       |
|:---------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------|
| Primary trigger      | Invariant boundary approach ($\dot{h} + \gamma_{\text{cbf}} h < 0$) or torque limit                                                                    | Human takeover assertion, monotonic lease timeout, or ODD exit   |
| Authority holder     | Autonomous policy retains proposal rights; enforcer modifies setpoints                                                                                 | Authority transferred to external entity or fallback controller  |
| Execution loop       | Fast inner control loop (`{python} InterventionSharedAuthorityScene.permission_rate_str` / $\le$ `{python} InterventionSharedAuthorityScene.tick_str`) | Same permission tick; protocol exchange spans multiple ticks     |
| Safety lease role    | Enforces continuous barrier satisfaction on admitted commands                                                                                          | Lease expiry invokes the state-dependent validated fallback      |
| Typical failure mode | Feasible set collapse; conservative deadlock or oscillation                                                                                            | Opposing commands cancel, mode confusion, or late human reaction |

: **Architectural boundaries of safety enforcement and supervisory intervention**: Enforcement operates in-loop as an active constraint on proposed actions; intervention transitions authority between discrete proposers. {#tbl-14-enforcement-vs-intervention tbl-colwidths="[20,40,40]"}

::: {#dfn-intervention-supervisory-intervention .callout-definition title="Supervisory intervention"}

***Supervisory intervention***\index{Intervention!definition}\index{Supervisory intervention!definition} is the transfer of the right to propose commands on named actuator channels between a learned policy and an authenticated person, committed on a control tick and bounded by a lease, while every command continues to pass the same permission check.

1.  **Significance**: The transfer is a delay on a moving machine, so it is priced in the stopping budget $d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$ rather than in the user interface. At the `{python} InterventionSharedAuthorityScene.v_str` aisle speed the `{python} InterventionSharedAuthorityScene.t_pause_str` design out-of-loop takeover carries the base `{python} InterventionSharedAuthorityScene.travel_str`, more than five times the `{python} InterventionSharedAuthorityScene.d_clear_str` rack-end clear distance.
2.  **Distinction**: Enforcement changes a proposal and leaves the proposer in place; intervention changes the proposer and leaves the check in place. A machine needs both, because neither can do the other's job.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that a takeover hands the operator the actuators. The operator gains only the right to propose, and the machine still needs a local stop that does not wait for the operator to act.

:::

### Capability matrices and the intervention-enforcement split {#sec-intervention-capability-split}

The capability matrix makes that distinction concrete on the warehouse mobile manipulator. The remote assistant can redirect motion, while the coworker accepting an item cannot.

```{python}
#| label: calc-intervention-coworker-handover
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COWORKER HANDOVER SPEED UNDER accept_item
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-intervention-human-authority, the capability example
# │          (veto_path and manual_drive for the remote assistant, accept_item
# │          for the coworker).
# │
# │ Goal:    Recall the handover cap that the enforcement record's handover
# │          entry holds (@sec-enforcement-telemetry owns it) and the contact
# │          ceilings derived in @sec-enforcement-intentional-contact
# │          (@eq-release-unbraked-force); no derivation here.
# │ Show:    Chosen TCP handover speed; the free-hand and clamped-hand ceilings.
# │ How:     calc_transient_contact_speed_limit with the ISO/TS 15066 Annex A hand
# │          body model (AISLE.k_contact_human, AISLE.m_contact_human) and the
# │          machine's effective mass, the same MLSysIM call the enforcement
# │          chapter's calc-enforcement-contact-force makes.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import meter, second, kilogram, newton, millimeter
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_transient_contact_speed_limit
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_velocity, fmt_force, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class InterventionCoworkerHandover:
    """Arm approach speed for the coworker's accept_item handover."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v_handover = AISLE.v_handover  # category: chosen
    k_hand = AISLE.k_contact_human  # category: datasheet (ISO/TS 15066 hand body model)
    m_hand = AISLE.m_contact_human  # category: datasheet (ISO/TS 15066 hand body model)
    f_criterion = AISLE.f_contact_criterion  # category: chosen
    m_eff = RM.arm_effective_contact_mass  # category: derived

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_ceiling = calc_transient_contact_speed_limit(f_criterion, m_eff, k_hand, human_mass=m_hand).to(meter / second)
    v_ceiling_clamped = calc_transient_contact_speed_limit(f_criterion, m_eff, k_hand).to(meter / second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v_ceiling.magnitude - 0.2415) < 5e-5, f"free-hand handover speed ceiling: {v_ceiling}")
    check(abs(v_ceiling_clamped.magnitude - 0.0527) < 5e-5, f"clamped-hand handover speed ceiling: {v_ceiling_clamped}")
    check(abs(m_eff.to(kilogram).magnitude - 12.0) < 1e-9, f"arm effective contact mass: {m_eff}")
    check(v_handover < v_ceiling, "The chosen handover speed must sit under the free-hand ceiling.")
    check(v_handover > v_ceiling_clamped, "The chosen handover speed must exceed the clamped ceiling, so clamping must be excluded.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(v_ceiling, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_ceiling_clamped_str = fmt_velocity(v_ceiling_clamped, unit=meter / second, precision=3)
    force_str = fmt_force(f_criterion)
```

For example, the remote assistant who supervises the mobile manipulator may hold a signed **trajectory veto** capability for the base's planner channel: role `remote_assistant`, operation `veto_path`, channel `planner_proposal`, preemption tier above the learned planner but below the local enforcer, authenticated session and nonce, and a clearance-derived acknowledgment deadline. The enforcer responds to a valid veto with a checked local hold or stop. The same session carries a second entry, `manual_drive`, on the base-velocity and arm-joint channels, which becomes active only through a handover that commits within the clearance-derived deadline, and lapses with the manual lease of @sec-intervention-authority-transitions; every command it carries still passes the permission check. A wheel drive-torque packet from that credential is denied, because neither entry grants the base's wheel drive-torque channel.

The coworker at the packing station holds a different entry, `accept_item`, which lets the coworker take from the gripper the mug the arm picked from the takeaway conveyor (@sec-intent, @sec-planning). That entry grants no motion authority. The item-handover channel of the enforcement record (@sec-enforcement-telemetry) caps the arm's approach to the coworker's hand at `{python} InterventionCoworkerHandover.v_handover_str`, and no capability lifts that cap. The handover is a collaborative application in the sense of ISO 10218-2:2025 [@iso10218part2], and the body model of the hand that bounds it, with the contact force that model predicts, is set out once in @sec-enforcement-intentional-contact. ISO 10218-2 leaves out the hazards of mounting the arm on a mobile platform, which ANSI/A3 R15.08-2 addresses for the running machine [@ansi1508part2].

The ceiling behind that cap comes from the contact-force model of @sec-enforcement-intentional-contact (@eq-release-unbraked-force). For a free hand, which recoils, the selected `{python} InterventionCoworkerHandover.force_str` criterion admits up to `{python} InterventionCoworkerHandover.v_ceiling_str`, and the cap sits under that ceiling. A hand clamped against a rack upright or the arm itself cannot recoil, and the same criterion then admits only `{python} InterventionCoworkerHandover.v_ceiling_clamped_str`, below the cap. The cap therefore holds only if the handover geometry excludes clamping, a premise the release case must evidence (@sec-release-question). The ceiling is conditional on these inputs and does not by itself establish a pressure or injury limit for a particular contact geometry; the site's risk assessment qualifies the effective mass, the force criterion, and the contact geometry before the cap is qualified.

Each capability entry binds actor, operation, channel, deadline, authentication, preemption tier, and fallback; a valid signature alone grants no motion authority. Of those fields, the deadline is the one the operator's own body sets, and it is the hardest to meet.

### Physiological reaction floors and kinematic drift {#sec-intervention-reaction-drift}

The remote assistant must notice the blocked aisle, decide how to recover, move the controls, and deliver a checked request. Summed in sequence, the total supervisory takeover latency $T_{\Sigma}$ is:
$$T_{\Sigma} = T_{\text{sensory}} + T_{\text{cognitive}} + T_{\text{motor}} + T_{\text{comm}}$$ {#eq-intervention-reaction-floor}
The first three terms belong to the person and depend on engagement and expectation; the last belongs to the console and the link. Human response times are distributions with long right tails, so a stopping budget needs a value that nearly every request meets, not the typical one. The calculation below compares a continuously engaged operator with an out-of-loop assistant. Its communication term includes transport and the protocol exchange, so that exchange must not be charged again.

Waiting consumes distance before the selected stop begins. The finished stopping budget from @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes supplies the machine delay, resident stop, and fixed allowances. Adding the human waiting interval exposes whether remote rescue can fit at the current speed; it does not authorize waiting when the local stop is already required.

```{python}
#| label: calc-intervention-admission-allocation
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE DISPATCH-TO-ADMISSION ALLOCATION CHARGED AGAINST THE TAKEOVER BUDGETS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-intervention-reaction-drift (the Delta_da paragraph),
# │          @sec-intervention-clearance-deadlines (the in-loop redesign),
# │          @sec-intervention-session-admission, @sec-intervention-authenticating-intervention,
# │          the verifier-flooding pitfall, and the summary.
# │
# │ Goal:    Charge the allocated Delta_da of @sec-placement to the chapter's
# │          partial ledgers and show which verdicts change.
# │ Show:    Delta_da and its aisle-speed ceiling; the waiting it leaves at the
# │          aisle speed; the retired 0.8 m/s slow-down's remainder before and
# │          after the charge (it missed by 5.0 ms); the Delta_da-charged in-loop
# │          ceiling (0.797 m/s) and the derived slow-down under it (0.75 m/s)
# │          with its remainder; the out-of-loop ceiling with Delta_da added;
# │          the travel Delta_da costs at the slow-down.
# │ How:     Delta_da is AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission (MLSysIM), the same value
# │          calc-placement-transport-budget imports (@sec-placement,
# │          nbk-placement-transport-budget). The slow-down is
# │          AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop: the charged ceiling rounded down to
# │          AISLE.v_takeover_resolution. Ceilings by
# │          calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity with T_Sigma + Delta_da in
# │          tau_delay.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg, meter, second, millimeter, millisecond
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_c2_stop_suffix,
    calc_scurve_stop_distance,
    calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity,
)
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class InterventionAdmissionAllocation:
    """The allocated dispatch-to-admission interval charged to the takeover ledgers."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
    v_in = AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop  # category: derived (charged ceiling rounded down to the resolution)
    v_step = AISLE.v_takeover_resolution  # category: chosen
    v_in_old = 0.8 * meter / second  # category: chosen (the retired slow-down, shown to explain the change)
    v_ool = AISLE.v_takeover_out_of_loop  # category: chosen
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative
    j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(RM.base.max_velocity, AISLE.a_brake)["peak_jerk"]  # category: derived (stipulated jerk bound)
    overhead = AISLE.fixed_overhead  # category: illustrative / chosen
    t_in = AISLE.t_takeover_in_loop  # category: derived (sourced human + transport)
    t_ool = AISLE.t_takeover_out_of_loop  # category: derived (sourced human + transport)
    # The @sec-placement allocation (calc-placement-transport-budget), from MLSysIM
    delta_da = AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission  # category: illustrative (allocation, not a measurement)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────

    def _t_latest(speed, *, _d=d_clear, _tau=tau_delay, _a=a_brake, _j=j_brake, _o=overhead):
        budget = speed * _tau + calc_scurve_stop_distance(speed, _a, _j) + _o
        return ((_d - budget) / speed).to(millisecond)

    def _ceiling(t, *, _d=d_clear, _tau=tau_delay, _a=a_brake, _j=j_brake):
        return calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(_d, _tau + t, _a, _j, AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track, AISLE.delta_margin).to(meter / second)

    t_ceiling = _t_latest(v)  # the most Delta_da the aisle-speed spare can pay for
    left_aisle = (t_ceiling - delta_da).to(millisecond)
    left_old = (_t_latest(v_in_old) - t_in).to(millisecond)
    short_old = (delta_da - left_old).to(millisecond)
    left_in = (_t_latest(v_in) - t_in).to(millisecond)
    left_in_da = (left_in - delta_da).to(millisecond)
    travel_da_in = (v_in * delta_da).to(millimeter)
    ceil_in_da = _ceiling(t_in + delta_da)
    ceil_ool_da = _ceiling(t_ool + delta_da)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(delta_da.to(millisecond).magnitude - 63.31072) < 1e-6, f"allocation must match @sec-placement: {delta_da}")
    check(abs(t_ceiling.magnitude - 100.775) < 5e-3, f"aisle-speed ceiling on Delta_da: {t_ceiling}")
    check(abs(left_aisle.magnitude - 37.464) < 5e-3, f"waiting left at the aisle speed: {left_aisle}")
    check(abs(left_old.magnitude - 58.275) < 5e-3, f"0.8 m/s in-loop remainder before the charge: {left_old}")
    check(abs(short_old.magnitude - 5.036) < 5e-3, f"the retired 0.8 m/s misses by 5.0 ms once charged: {short_old}")
    check(abs(ceil_in_da.magnitude - AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop_ceiling.magnitude) < 1e-9, "Charged ceiling matches the registry.")
    check(abs(ceil_in_da.magnitude - 0.797) < 5e-4, f"Delta_da-charged in-loop ceiling: {ceil_in_da}")
    check(v_in < ceil_in_da < v_in + v_step, "The slow-down is the charged ceiling rounded down to the resolution.")
    check(left_in_da.magnitude > 0, "Charged with Delta_da, the derived in-loop slow-down now meets its deadline.")
    check(v_ool < ceil_ool_da, "The crawl must survive the Delta_da charge.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    delta_da_str = fmt_latency(delta_da, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_ceiling_str = fmt_latency(t_ceiling, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    left_aisle_str = fmt_latency(left_aisle, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    left_old_str = fmt_latency(left_old, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    short_old_str = fmt_latency(short_old, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    left_in_str = fmt_latency(left_in, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    left_in_da_str = fmt_latency(left_in_da, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    travel_da_in_str = fmt_length(travel_da_in, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    ceil_in_da_str = fmt_velocity(ceil_in_da, unit=meter / second, precision=3)
    ceil_ool_da_str = fmt_velocity(ceil_ool_da, unit=meter / second, precision=3)
    v_in_old_str = fmt_velocity(v_in_old, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    v_step_str = fmt_velocity(v_step, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_in_str = fmt_velocity(v_in, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_ool_str = fmt_velocity(v_ool, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
```

The budgets that follow are illustrative design comparisons, not measured takeover performance. Their displayed remainders exclude $\Delta_{\text{da}}$, the dispatch-to-admission interval, because @sec-placement budgets it separately: an allocation of `{python} InterventionAdmissionAllocation.delta_da_str`, not yet measured, against the `{python} InterventionAdmissionAllocation.t_ceiling_str` that the aisle-speed spare can pay for (\ref{nbk-placement-transport-budget}). At speed $v$ the usable spare is the displayed spare less $v\Delta_{\text{da}}$, so at the aisle speed only `{python} InterventionAdmissionAllocation.left_aisle_str` of waiting survives the charge. Each budget below first shows the partial ledger and then states what the charge changes; @sec-intervention-clearance-deadlines states which clock origin each budget uses.

```{python}
#| label: calc-intervention-operator-takeover-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ OPERATOR TAKEOVER AGAINST THE MACHINE'S STOPPING BUDGET
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-intervention-human-authority, the two takeover modes that
# │          follow @eq-intervention-reaction-floor, and the notebook
# │          "Takeover budget and clearance margin".
# │
# │ Goal:    Price an operator's sourced takeover delay on the warehouse mobile
# │          manipulator at its aisle speed.
# │ Show:    Spare margin at 1.3 m/s; the in-loop decomposition (Model Human
# │          Processor at the slow end of each cycle, video glass-to-glass
# │          latency, four-phase exchange); the out-of-loop design value
# │          (90th-percentile condition-mean take-over time plus the same
# │          transport); travel during each; the stop with each delay added;
# │          the speed ceilings.
# │ How:     Finished stopping budget from the WarehouseAisle scenario
# │          (jerk-limited resident stop, all overheads); the jerk bound is the
# │          peak jerk of the reference C2 polynomial at the drive limit
# │          (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix); T_Sigma adds to tau_delay;
# │          ceilings by calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import meter, second, millimeter, millisecond
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_c2_stop_suffix,
    calc_scurve_stop_distance,
    calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity,
)
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_length,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_magnitude,
    fmt_multiple,
    fmt_display_math,
    fmt_acceleration,
    fmt_jerk,
    check,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class InterventionTakeoverBudget:
    """Operator takeover delay spent against the finished stopping budget."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative
    j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(RM.base.max_velocity, AISLE.a_brake)["peak_jerk"]  # category: derived (stipulated jerk bound)
    near_overhead = AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track  # category: illustrative
    margin = AISLE.delta_margin  # category: chosen
    overhead = AISLE.fixed_overhead  # category: illustrative / chosen
    t_sensory = AISLE.t_human_perceptual_slow  # category: sourced (Card, Moran, Newell 1983)
    t_cognitive = AISLE.t_human_cognitive_slow  # category: sourced
    t_motor = AISLE.t_human_motor_slow  # category: sourced
    t_video = AISLE.t_video_glass_to_glass  # category: sourced (wired best case)
    t_handshake = AISLE.t_handshake  # category: chosen (four-phase budgets)
    t_expected = AISLE.t_brake_response_expected  # category: sourced (Green 2000)
    t_surprise = AISLE.t_brake_response_surprise  # category: sourced (Green 2000)
    t_tot_mean = AISLE.t_takeover_driving_mean  # category: sourced (Zhang et al. 2019)
    t_tot_p90 = AISLE.t_takeover_driving_p90  # category: sourced (computed from its data)
    t_in = AISLE.t_takeover_in_loop  # category: derived
    t_ool = AISLE.t_takeover_out_of_loop  # category: derived
    # Source: UN Regulation No. 157 (ALKS), para. 5.4.4.1: a minimum risk
    # manoeuvre starts at the earliest 10 s after the transition demand.
    # Promotion candidate: literature registry.
    t_r157 = 10 * second  # category: sourced

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    reaction = (v * tau_delay).to(millimeter)
    r157_over_ool = (t_r157 / t_ool).to("").magnitude
    travel_r157 = (v * t_r157).to(meter)
    stop = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v, a_brake, j_brake).to(millimeter)
    budget = (reaction + stop + overhead).to(millimeter)
    spare = (d_clear - budget).to(millimeter)
    t_comm = (t_video + t_handshake).to(millisecond)
    t_sum = (t_sensory + t_cognitive + t_motor + t_comm).to(millisecond)
    travel_in = (v * t_in).to(millimeter)
    travel_ool = (v * t_ool).to(millimeter)
    d_stop_in = (budget + travel_in).to(millimeter)
    d_stop_ool = (budget + travel_ool).to(millimeter)
    stop_ratio = (d_stop_ool / d_stop_in).to("").magnitude
    # Napkin-math box "The takeover tax": the overruns and the waiting-to-spare ratio.
    overrun_in = (d_stop_in - d_clear).to(millimeter)
    overrun_ool = (d_stop_ool - d_clear).to(millimeter)
    travel_over_spare = (travel_in / spare).to("").magnitude

    def _ceiling(t, *, _d=d_clear, _tau=tau_delay, _a=a_brake, _j=j_brake, _n=near_overhead, _m=margin):
        return calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(_d, _tau + t, _a, _j, _n, _m).to(meter / second)

    ceil_in = _ceiling(t_in)
    ceil_ool = _ceiling(t_ool)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(spare.magnitude - 131.01) < 5e-3, f"spare margin at the aisle speed: {spare}")
    check(abs(t_sum.magnitude - t_in.to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "The four stages must sum to the in-loop takeover.")
    check(abs((t_tot_p90 + t_comm - t_ool).to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "The out-of-loop takeover is the p90 time plus transport.")
    check(travel_in > 5 * spare, "The in-loop takeover must overrun the spare margin several times at the aisle speed.")
    check(travel_ool > 5 * d_clear, "The out-of-loop travel must exceed five times the clear distance.")
    check(abs(d_stop_in.magnitude - 1755.49) < 5e-3, f"stop with in-loop takeover: {d_stop_in}")
    check(abs(d_stop_ool.magnitude - 6773.49) < 5e-3, f"stop with out-of-loop takeover: {d_stop_ool}")
    check(abs(ceil_in.magnitude - 0.8362) < 5e-5, f"in-loop takeover ceiling: {ceil_in}")
    check(abs(ceil_ool.magnitude - 0.1911) < 5e-5, f"out-of-loop takeover ceiling: {ceil_ool}")
    check(abs(stop_ratio - 3.86) < 0.01, f"out-of-loop to in-loop stop ratio: {stop_ratio}")
    check(abs(r157_over_ool - 2.24) < 0.01, f"R157 transition over the design takeover: {r157_over_ool}")
    check(abs(travel_r157.magnitude - 13.0) < 1e-9, f"travel at aisle speed during the R157 transition: {travel_r157}")
    check(abs(budget.magnitude - 968.99) < 5e-3, f"machine-alone stop at the aisle speed: {budget}")
    check(abs(overrun_in.magnitude - 655.49) < 5e-3, f"in-loop overrun: {overrun_in}")
    check(abs(travel_over_spare - 6.0) < 0.05, f"in-loop travel over the spare: {travel_over_spare}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    spare_str = fmt_length(spare, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_in_str = fmt_latency(t_in, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_ool_str = fmt_latency(t_ool, unit=second, precision=1)
    t_sensory_str = fmt_latency(t_sensory, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_cognitive_str = fmt_latency(t_cognitive, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_motor_str = fmt_latency(t_motor, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_video_str = fmt_latency(t_video, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_handshake_str = fmt_latency(t_handshake, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_comm_str = fmt_latency(t_comm, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_expected_str = fmt_latency(t_expected, unit=second, precision=2)
    t_surprise_str = fmt_latency(t_surprise, unit=second, precision=1)
    t_tot_mean_str = fmt_latency(t_tot_mean, unit=second, precision=2)
    t_tot_p90_str = fmt_latency(t_tot_p90, unit=second, precision=2)
    travel_in_str = fmt_length(travel_in, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    travel_ool_str = fmt_length(travel_ool, unit=meter, precision=2)
    d_stop_in_str = fmt_length(d_stop_in, unit=meter, precision=2)
    d_stop_ool_str = fmt_length(d_stop_ool, unit=meter, precision=2)
    stop_mult_str = fmt_multiple(stop_ratio, precision=1)
    ceil_in_str = fmt_velocity(ceil_in, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    ceil_ool_str = fmt_velocity(ceil_ool, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    t_r157_str = fmt_latency(t_r157, unit=second, precision=0)
    r157_mult_str = fmt_multiple(r157_over_ool, precision=1)
    travel_r157_str = fmt_length(travel_r157, unit=meter, precision=0)
    tau_delay_str = fmt_latency(tau_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    j_brake_str = fmt_jerk(j_brake, unit=meter / second**3, precision=2)
    overhead_str = fmt_length(overhead, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    budget_str = fmt_length(budget, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    overrun_in_str = fmt_length(overrun_in, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    overrun_ool_str = fmt_length(overrun_ool, unit=meter, precision=2)
    travel_over_spare_mult_str = fmt_multiple(travel_over_spare, precision=1)

    reaction_value_str = fmt_magnitude(reaction, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    stop_value_str = fmt_magnitude(stop, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    overhead_value_str = fmt_magnitude(overhead, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    travel_in_value_str = fmt_magnitude(travel_in, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    travel_ool_value_str = fmt_magnitude(travel_ool, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    d_stop_in_value_str = fmt_magnitude(d_stop_in, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    d_stop_ool_value_str = fmt_magnitude(d_stop_ool, unit=millimeter, precision=2)

    haptic_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"d_{{\text{{stop}},1}} = v\,\tau_{{\text{{delay}}}} + v\,T_{{\Sigma,1}} + d_{{\text{{suffix}}}}(v) + \delta = "
        rf"{reaction_value_str} + {travel_in_value_str} + {stop_value_str} + {overhead_value_str} = {d_stop_in_value_str}\text{{ mm}}"
    )
    ool_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"d_{{\text{{stop}},2}} = v\,\tau_{{\text{{delay}}}} + v\,T_{{\Sigma,2}} + d_{{\text{{suffix}}}}(v) + \delta = "
        rf"{reaction_value_str} + {travel_ool_value_str} + {stop_value_str} + {overhead_value_str} = {d_stop_ool_value_str}\text{{ mm}}"
    )
    machine_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"d_{{\text{{stop}},0}} = v\,\tau_{{\text{{delay}}}} + d_{{\text{{suffix}}}}(v) + \delta = "
        rf"{reaction_value_str} + {stop_value_str} + {overhead_value_str} = {fmt_magnitude(budget, unit=millimeter, precision=2)}\text{{ mm}}"
    )
```

The finished stopping budget of @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes (@tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget) shows what @eq-intervention-reaction-floor costs on the mobile manipulator. At the `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.v_str` aisle speed it leaves `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.spare_str` of the `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.d_clear_str` rack-end clear distance. A takeover delay adds to the machine's own pre-brake delay $\tau_{\text{delay}}$, and every millisecond of it becomes travel at the aisle speed:

1. **Mode 1: Continuous in-loop teleoperation**: An attending operator with hands on the controls of a synchronized leader arm or a real-time console, responding to the stimulus the task has led them to expect, makes a simple reaction. The Model Human Processor[^fn-model-human-processor] [@card1983psychology] prices that reaction as one perceptual, one cognitive, and one motor cycle [@jastrzembski2007model]; at the slow end of each cycle's range, $T_{\text{sensory}} =$ `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_sensory_str`, $T_{\text{cognitive}} =$ `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_cognitive_str`, and $T_{\text{motor}} =$ `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_motor_str`. The console adds $T_{\text{comm}} =$ `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_comm_str`: the scene reaches the operator after a video glass-to-glass latency[^fn-video-glass-latency] of `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_video_str`, measured for a wired teleoperation link [@schimpe2022opensource], and the request returns through the `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_handshake_str` protocol exchange of @tbl-14-handshake-protocol. By @eq-intervention-reaction-floor, $T_{\Sigma,1} =$ `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_in_str`. The machine travels `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.travel_in_str` during that delay, several times the spare margin. Solving the budget for speed with $T_{\Sigma,1}$ added to $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ bounds the machine to `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.ceil_in_str`. The value holds only for the expected stimulus. A driver who is waiting for a brake signal needs up to `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_expected_str` to detect it and reach the pedal, and a surprise raises that to about `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_surprise_str` [@green2000stop]. @Sec-intervention-speed-ceilings prices those cases.
2. **Mode 2: Passive out-of-the-loop supervisory takeover**: An assistant who monitors the telemetry of several machines passively does not make a simple reaction, and its stages cannot be priced separately. Driver take-over studies measure the whole interval, from the take-over request to the first control input. Across 520 experimental conditions in 129 studies, the mean take-over time averaged `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_tot_mean_str`, and the distribution of those condition means is skewed to the right [@zhang2019takeover]. A stopping budget must hold for nearly every request, so the design value is the 90th percentile of the condition means, `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_tot_p90_str`, computed from the study's published data. With the same `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_comm_str` console term, the takeover delay is $T_{\Sigma,2} =$ `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_ool_str`, during which the machine covers `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.travel_ool_str`, more than five times the clear distance, before any brake command. The same solution bounds the machine to `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.ceil_ool_str`.

[^fn-model-human-processor]: **Model Human Processor**\index{Model Human Processor!slow bound}: @card1983psychology modeled a person responding to a stimulus as three processors in series, perceptual, cognitive, and motor, and gave each cycle time a typical value and a range rather than a single number. The range is the design input. A budget built on the typical cycles admits a speed that a slower but still normal operator overruns, so this chapter's design row takes the slow end of every range.

[^fn-video-glass-latency]: **Glass-to-Glass Latency**\index{Glass-to-glass latency!teleoperation}: The interval from light entering the remote camera's lens to the matching image leaving the operator's display, covering exposure, encoding, transport, decoding, and display refresh. It is the only video delay the operator experiences, and every stage of that path contributes to it, so a value measured on a wired link does not carry over to a warehouse wireless link. The site must measure its own link before the value enters the takeover budget.

In Mode 2 at the aisle speed, the machine would reach a static obstacle at the rack end at full speed, because contact occurs before braking ever begins. Stronger braking can raise a finite stopping-speed ceiling, but cannot recover distance already spent waiting. As braking distance tends toward zero, reaction travel still sets a limiting ceiling. A percentile of condition means also understates the tail an individual operator can produce, because each condition's own spread grows with its mean; the site must measure its operators, console, and task load before any of these values admits a speed. Road regulation sizes the same interval generously for a vehicle that can keep driving while it waits. An automated lane-keeping system approved under UN Regulation No. 157 may begin its own minimum risk manoeuvre no earlier than `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_r157_str` after it issues a transition demand [@unece2021r157], `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.r157_mult_str` the design takeover here. The vehicle can afford that wait because it stays in its lane under automated control throughout. At the aisle speed the same wait would carry the mobile manipulator `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.travel_r157_str`, so the machine cannot borrow the road's interval, only its structure of a demand, a bounded wait, and an automatic fallback. @Sec-intervention-clearance-deadlines turns the two design values into the speeds at which the machine may request each kind of takeover.

@Fig-14-in-loop-takeover-strip lays the Mode 1 stages end to end on one time axis. The operator's three cycles fill most of it, the `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_handshake_str` protocol exchange only the last sliver, and the distance row beneath converts the same interval into the `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.travel_in_str` the machine covers at the aisle speed against its `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.spare_str` spare.

::: {#fig-14-in-loop-takeover-strip fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Where an in-loop takeover spends its time**: The `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_in_str` in-loop takeover drawn to scale from the request, stage by stage: video transport to the console, the operator's perceptual, cognitive, and motor cycles at the slow end of the Model Human Processor, and the four-phase handshake that ends at commit. The distance row converts the same axis into travel at the `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.v_str` aisle speed; the bracket at its left marks the `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.spare_str` spare, which the machine exhausts within the video stage." fig-alt="Timing strip with three lanes over 0 to about 630 milliseconds. The console lane holds a video interval from 0 to 104 milliseconds. The operator lane holds perceive 200, decide 170, and act 100 milliseconds end to end, ending at 574. The permission lane holds a 31 millisecond handshake ending at commit at 605 milliseconds. A bracket above spans the whole 605 millisecond takeover. A distance row below, labeled travel at 1.30 meters per second, carries a bracket of 786 millimeters across the whole interval and a short bracket of 131 millimeters of spare ending near 101 milliseconds."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ IN-LOOP TAKEOVER TIMING STRIP (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-14-in-loop-takeover-strip
# │
# │ Goal: Draw the Mode 1 takeover stages on one to-scale time axis with the
# │       travel they cost at the aisle speed.
# │ Show: video 104 + perceive 200 + decide 170 + act 100 + handshake 31
# │       = 605 ms; 786.5 mm of travel at 1.3 m/s against the 131.0 mm spare.
# │ How: the shared viz.takeover_strip builder reads the scenario terms;
# │      InterventionTakeoverBudget supplies the speed and the spare.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond
from mlsysim.fmt import check
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

TB = InterventionTakeoverBudget

# ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
v = TB.v  # category: chosen (aisle speed)
spare = TB.spare  # category: derived
t_spare = (spare / v).to(millisecond).magnitude  # category: derived

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
strip = viz.takeover_strip(AISLE, speed=v)
strip.brackets = list(strip.brackets) + [
    viz.Bracket(0, t_spare, f"{spare.magnitude:.0f} mm spare", "structural", "distance", 1),
]
t_commit = max(e.t for e in strip.events)

# ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(t_commit - TB.t_in.to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "The strip must end at the in-loop takeover.")
check(t_spare < TB.t_video.to(millisecond).magnitude, "The spare must be spent within the video stage.")

# ┌── 4. PLOT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax, axd = viz.plot_timing_strip(strip)
plt.show()
```

:::

::: {#nbk-intervention-operator-takeover-budget-spatial-clearance-margin .callout-notebook title="The takeover tax"}

**Problem**: At the `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.v_str` aisle speed, does the finished stopping budget still fit the rack-end clear distance once an in-loop or an out-of-loop takeover delay is inserted before braking, and by how much does each overrun it?

**Variables**:

* $v =$ `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.v_str` (Chosen) and $D_{\text{clear}} =$ `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.d_clear_str` (Illustrative).
* $\tau_{\text{delay}} =$ `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.tau_delay_str`, the machine's own pre-brake delay (Derived; @tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget), which excludes the dispatch-to-admission travel $v\,\Delta_{\text{da}}$ this chapter charges separately.
* $d_{\text{suffix}}(v) = v^2/(2a_{\text{brake}}) + v\,a_{\text{brake}}/(2j_{\max})$, the jerk-limited resident stop of @eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix, with $a_{\text{brake}} =$ `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.a_brake_str` (Illustrative) and $j_{\max} =$ `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.j_brake_str` (Derived).
* $\delta = \delta_{\text{loc}} + \delta_{\text{margin}} + \epsilon_{\text{track}} =$ `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.overhead_str` (Illustrative and Chosen).
* $T_{\Sigma,1} =$ `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_in_str` in-loop and $T_{\Sigma,2} =$ `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_ool_str` out-of-loop (Derived, from the measured human and transport terms of Modes 1 and 2 plus the chosen handshake).

**Math**: Every term is in millimeters. The machine alone leaves the `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.spare_str` spare:

`{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.machine_display_math`

Each takeover adds $v\,T_{\Sigma}$ before the same stop:

`{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.haptic_display_math`

`{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.ool_display_math`

**Result**: The in-loop takeover overruns the clear distance by `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.overrun_in_str` and the out-of-loop takeover by `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.overrun_ool_str`; the second stop is `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.stop_mult_str` the first.

**Systems insight**: The waiting term, not the braking term, decides the verdict. The in-loop takeover alone covers `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.travel_over_spare_mult_str` the spare, so no stronger brake can make $d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$ hold at this speed; only a lower $v$ or a stop before the request can. The kinematic derivation of the stop terms is in @sec-appendix-systems-stopping.

:::

### Speed ceilings and the clearance collision horizon {#sec-intervention-speed-ceilings}

@Fig-14-takeover-timeline draws the two design takeovers at the aisle speed. Every trace ends in the same resident stop; what separates them is how long the machine coasts before that stop begins. The warehouse comparison can include different operator states without changing machines. Each state is useful only at speeds where its response time leaves room for the same resident stop, and the sourced response times differ by more than an order of magnitude.

::: {#fig-14-takeover-timeline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Two takeovers against one clear distance**: Clearance consumed at the `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.v_str` aisle speed, starting from the fixed allowances. Each trace coasts through its delay and then follows the same jerk-limited resident stop. The machine alone stops `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.spare_str` short of the `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.d_clear_str` clear distance. A `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_in_str` in-loop takeover inserted before braking carries the stop to `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.d_stop_in_str`, and a `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_ool_str` out-of-loop takeover carries it to `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.d_stop_ool_str`. The waiting, not the braking, spends the clearance." fig-alt="Two panels of clearance consumed in meters against time in seconds. Three traces start at a shaded band of fixed allowances, rise linearly while the machine waits, and flatten during an identical braking curve. A dashed horizontal line marks the rack-end clear distance. The left panel shows the first two seconds: the machine-only trace ends below the line with a bracket marking the spare margin, and the in-loop takeover trace ends above it. The right panel shows six seconds and seven meters, where the out-of-loop takeover trace rises far above the line before braking."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TWO TAKEOVERS AGAINST ONE CLEAR DISTANCE (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-14-takeover-timeline
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that the takeover delay, not the braking, spends the clearance.
# │ Show:    Clearance consumed vs. time at the aisle speed for the machine
# │          alone, the in-loop takeover, and the out-of-loop takeover; the
# │          clear distance; the spare margin of the machine alone.
# │ How:     InterventionTakeoverBudget terms. Each trace starts at the fixed
# │          allowances, coasts for T_Sigma + tau_delay, then follows the
# │          jerk-limited resident stop (trapezoidal deceleration, a_brake,
# │          j_brake), integrated numerically and guarded against
# │          calc_scurve_stop_distance through the budget endpoints.
# │
# │ Imports: InterventionTakeoverBudget (calc-intervention-takeover-budget)
# │ Exports: (figure only)
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.core.units import meter, second, millimeter
from mlsysim.fmt import check

TB = InterventionTakeoverBudget

# ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
v = TB.v.to(meter / second).magnitude  # category: chosen
a = TB.a_brake.to(meter / second**2).magnitude  # category: illustrative
j = TB.j_brake.to(meter / second**3).magnitude  # category: derived
delta = TB.overhead.to(meter).magnitude  # category: illustrative / chosen
d_clear = TB.d_clear.to(meter).magnitude  # category: illustrative
tau = TB.tau_delay.to(second).magnitude  # category: derived
cases = [
    ("machine alone", 0.0),
    (f"in-loop takeover, {TB.t_in_str}", TB.t_in.to(second).magnitude),
    (f"out-of-loop takeover, {TB.t_ool_str}", TB.t_ool.to(second).magnitude),
]

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def stop_profile(dt=1e-4):
    """Speed and distance during the trapezoidal-deceleration stop from v."""
    t_j = a / j
    t_c = v / a - t_j
    t = np.arange(0.0, 2 * t_j + t_c + dt, dt)
    decel = np.where(t < t_j, j * t, np.where(t < t_j + t_c, a, np.clip(a - j * (t - t_j - t_c), 0.0, a)))
    speed = np.maximum(v - np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(0.5 * (decel[1:] + decel[:-1]) * dt)]), 0.0)
    dist = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(0.5 * (speed[1:] + speed[:-1]) * dt)])
    return t, dist

t_stop, d_stop = stop_profile()
traces = []
for name, t_take in cases:
    t_wait = t_take + tau
    t = np.concatenate([np.linspace(0.0, t_wait, 200), t_wait + t_stop])
    y = np.concatenate([delta + v * np.linspace(0.0, t_wait, 200), delta + v * t_wait + d_stop])
    traces.append((name, t_wait, t, y))

# ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ends = [tr[3][-1] for tr in traces]
check(abs(ends[0] - TB.budget.to(meter).magnitude) < 1e-4, "machine-alone trace must end at the finished budget")
check(abs(ends[1] - TB.d_stop_in.to(meter).magnitude) < 1e-4, "in-loop trace must end at the in-loop stop")
check(abs(ends[2] - TB.d_stop_ool.to(meter).magnitude) < 1e-4, "out-of-loop trace must end at the out-of-loop stop")
check(ends[0] < d_clear < ends[1], "only the machine-alone trace fits the clear distance")

# ┌── 4. PLOT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

viz.set_book_style()
C = viz.COLORS
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.4), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.1]})
styles = [
    dict(color=C["GreenLine"], ls="-", lw=2.0),
    dict(color=C["BlueLine"], ls="--", lw=2.0),
    dict(color=C["BrownLine"], ls="-.", lw=2.0),
]
panels = [(axes[0], 1.9, 2.0, "(a) First 1.9 s"), (axes[1], 6.0, 7.2, "(b) Full out-of-loop takeover")]
for ax, t_max, y_max, title in panels:
    ax.axhspan(0.0, delta, color=C["grid"], alpha=0.35, lw=0, zorder=1)
    ax.axhline(d_clear, color=C["RedLine"], ls=(0, (5, 3)), lw=1.4, zorder=2)
    for k, ((name, t_wait, t, y), st) in enumerate(zip(traces, styles)):
        ax.plot(t, y, label=name, zorder=6 - k, **st)
        if t_wait < t_max:
            ax.plot([t_wait], [delta + v * t_wait], "o", ms=5, color=st["color"], zorder=9)
    ax.set_xlim(0.0, t_max)
    ax.set_ylim(0.0, y_max)
    ax.set_xlabel("time since the hazard appears (s)")
    ax.set_title(title, loc="left", fontsize=10.5)
axes[0].set_ylabel("clearance consumed (m)")

ax = axes[0]
ax.text(1.88, d_clear + 0.03, f"clear distance {TB.d_clear_str}", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=C["RedLine"])
ax.text(1.88, delta / 2, "fixed allowances", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=C["primary"])
t_end0 = traces[0][2][-1]
x_br = t_end0 + 0.08
ax.annotate("", xy=(x_br, d_clear), xytext=(x_br, ends[0]), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=C["primary"], lw=0.9))
ax.text(x_br + 0.04, (d_clear + ends[0]) / 2, f"{TB.spare_str} spare", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=C["primary"])
ax.text(traces[1][2][-1], ends[1] - 0.07, f"stops at {TB.d_stop_in_str}", ha="right", va="top", fontsize=8.5, color=C["BlueLine"])
ax.text(0.05, 1.93, "dots: braking begins", ha="left", va="top", fontsize=8.5, color=C["primary"])
ax.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.0, 0.92), fontsize=8.5, frameon=False)

ax = axes[1]
ax.text(5.95, d_clear + 0.08, f"clear distance {TB.d_clear_str}", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=C["RedLine"])
ax.text(traces[2][2][-1] - 0.05, ends[2] + 0.12, f"stops at {TB.d_stop_ool_str}", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=C["BrownLine"])
ax.text(
    2.1,
    delta + v * 2.1 + 0.25,
    f"{TB.travel_ool_str} of travel\nbefore any brake command",
    ha="right",
    va="bottom",
    fontsize=8.5,
    color=C["BrownLine"],
)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
